title: Variational Corrections to Strong-Disorder Renormalization in the Two-Dimensional Random Transverse Field Ising Model on Quantum Hardware
authors: Alina Joch, Benedikt Fauseweh
abstract: Strong-disorder renormalization-group (SDRG) methods provide an effective description of disordered quantum many-body systems by identifying the dominant couplings for the low energy physics. However, the resulting renormalization-group flow is approximate and neglects correlations beyond the RG description. Here, we investigate whether variational quantum optimization can be used to correct these approximations. Building on the emergent-coupling-based ansatz (ECBA) developed for the one-dimensional random Heisenberg model, we introduce a formulation adapted to the two-dimensional random transverse field Ising model. The SDRG flow determines the structure of the circuit, while variational optimization allows the state to deviate from the RG approximation. We study the resulting ansatz numerically and experimentally on an IQM superconducting quantum processor. For a 16-qubit system, we perform full variational optimization on the quantum processor, while a 49-qubit system is investigated using pre-optimized parameters, achieving a relative energy accuracy of 89% and 97%, respectively. Our results demonstrate that RG information can be translated into shallow, hardware-compatible quantum circuits while variational optimization enables corrections beyond the underlying RG approximation also for two-dimensional systems.

infographic.key_insight: Variational quantum optimization can correct strong-disorder renormalization-group approximations using shallow circuits tailored to a two-dimensional disordered Ising model.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Renormalization-group structure provides a physics-informed route to hardware-compatible circuits for simulating disordered quantum systems.
method: Adapt the emergent-coupling-based ansatz to the two-dimensional random transverse field Ising model.
Use the SDRG flow to determine circuit structure.
Optimize circuit parameters to capture correlations beyond the SDRG approximation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical and IQM superconducting-hardware studies report relative energy accuracies of 89% for 16 qubits with full on-device optimization and 97% for 49 qubits using pre-optimized parameters.
infographic.watch_item: The 49-qubit experiment uses pre-optimized parameters, so it does not demonstrate full variational optimization at that scale.
infographic.paper_title: Variational Corrections to Strong-Disorder Renormalization in the Two-Dimensional Random Transverse Field Ising Model on Quantum Hardware

title: Generative Models using Multi-layer Quantum Extreme Learning Machines
authors: Amir Azzam, M. Pilar Casado, Michele Grossi, Arnau Riera, Sofia Vallecorsa
abstract: Quantum reservoir computing (QRC) and the closely related quantum extreme learning machine (QELM) paradigm exploit the complex dynamics of an uncontrolled quantum system for machine learning, offering an alternative to variational quantum algorithms whose training is hindered by barren plateaus and costly circuit optimization. Because the quantum system itself is left fixed, learning reduces to fitting a linear readout of a set of measured observables, and no gradient is ever taken through the quantum device. In this work we repurpose this paradigm for generative modeling: a fixed, randomly initialized multi-layer QELM transforms a scalar latent variable into a rich vector of measured expectation values, and only a simple linear readout is trained to map these to samples of a target distribution. The readout is fitted by minimizing the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) between generated and target samples. We show that this algorithm is capable of reproducing a range of one- and two-dimensional distributions. Moreover, encoding the class label on dedicated qubits enables conditional generation of different classes of distributions with the same linear readout. We show that this cannot be achieved by the linear readout alone, and that the reservoir dynamics play a role in the ability to distinguish the different classes of distributions. We also show that using a simple six-qubit reservoir one is able to generate handwritten digits from the Digits and MNIST datasets with high accuracy. Moreover, replacing the Haar-random dynamics by time evolution under several physical Hamiltonians leaves the performance unchanged, provided the evolution spreads the input across the register. Finally, we show that a classical random Fourier feature model of the same size performs equally well: at the sizes we study, the QELM offers no advantage over its classical counterpart.

infographic.key_insight: A fixed multi-layer quantum extreme learning machine can generate distributions and handwritten digits by training only a linear readout, but shows no advantage over matched classical random Fourier features at the studied sizes.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Keeping quantum dynamics fixed avoids quantum-circuit optimization and gradients through the device, simplifying training while retaining quantum measurement requirements.
method: Encode a scalar latent variable into a fixed, randomly initialized multi-layer quantum reservoir and measure expectation values.
Train a linear readout by minimizing maximum mean discrepancy between generated and target samples.
Encode class labels on dedicated qubits for conditional generation with a shared readout.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluations cover one- and two-dimensional distributions and six-qubit generation of Digits and MNIST images; physical Hamiltonian dynamics preserve performance when they spread inputs across the register.
infographic.watch_item: Quantum advantage is not demonstrated: a same-size classical random Fourier feature model performs equally well in the reported evaluations.
infographic.paper_title: Generative Models using Multi-layer Quantum Extreme Learning Machines

title: Rate-1/2 Quantum LDPC Codes for Multi-tier Superconducting Hardware
authors: Jiaxuan Zhang, Zhao-Yun Chen, Jia-Ning Li, Tian-Hao Wei, Qing-Yang Hou, Wei-Cheng Kong
abstract: Quantum error correction is essential for scalable quantum computing, while its resource overhead is governed in large part by the encoding rate, namely the number of logical qubits encoded per physical data qubit. Recent quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) constructions have entered the ultra-high-rate regime with encoding rates above 1/2, but their syndrome-extraction circuits generally rely on reconfigurable connectivity or long-range qubit transport, making them difficult to implement on fixed-connectivity superconducting hardware. Here we introduce Armillary codes, a family of ultra-high-rate qLDPC codes whose algebraic structure is generated by native iSWAP routing under hardware constraints. The construction jointly enforces stabilizer commutation and correct parallel syndrome extraction, while admitting radial and circumferential couplings in crossing-free routing layers. We construct explicit codes with rates above 1/2, stabilizer weight 12, Tanner-graph girth 6, and distances from 12 to 16, with layouts on 5 or 6 hardware tiers. Compared with the Gross and Mitten codes at the same distances, the Armillary codes achieve encoding rates about 6 and 2.5 times those of the Gross and Mitten codes, respectively, while maintaining lower hardware-complexity scores. In circuit-level simulations, the \([\![8688,4348,16]\!]\) code approaches the teraquop regime, achieving a logical error rate of \(1.62\times10^{-12}\) per logical qubit per round at a physical error rate of 0.1\%. These results show that the rate-\(1/2\) regime of qLDPC codes can be extended from reconfigurable platforms to superconducting hardware, providing a route toward low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum processors.

infographic.key_insight: Armillary qLDPC codes encode more than one logical qubit per two physical data qubits while supporting fixed-connectivity, multi-tier superconducting layouts.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The design offers a path to lower data-qubit overhead without requiring reconfigurable connectivity or long-range qubit transport.
method: Generate code structure through hardware-constrained native iSWAP routing.
Jointly enforce stabilizer commutation and correct parallel syndrome extraction.
Use radial and circumferential couplings in crossing-free routing layers across 5–6 hardware tiers.
infographic.evidence_signal: Circuit-level simulations of the [[8688,4348,16]] code report a logical error rate of 1.62×10⁻¹² per logical qubit per round at a physical error rate of 0.1%.
infographic.watch_item: The results are simulation-based; practical performance still depends on realizing reliable multi-tier couplings and iSWAP routing in superconducting hardware.
infographic.paper_title: Rate-1/2 Quantum LDPC Codes for Multi-tier Superconducting Hardware

title: Agentic AI for Discovering Fault-Tolerant Quantum Circuits
authors: Aritra Lahiri, Florian Marquardt
abstract: Scaling quantum computing toward practical quantum advantage is currently limited by the efficiency of circuits that operate on information encoded by quantum error-correcting codes. The full stack of quantum computing encompasses several tasks: preparation of logical code states, implementation of logical gates, logical routines on encoded qubits, etc. Yet, these circuits are largely designed by hand for individual cases, with some recent works incorporating machine learning for certain aspects. We formulate this problem as agentic evolutionary program synthesis, wherein a large language model, leveraging its pretraining knowledge and tool-use proficiency, and guided by a circuit verifier, evolves a program that defines a Clifford circuit for a wide range of curated tasks such as logical state preparation, logical gate design, and logical routines such as code-switching, code growth, etc. Our approach consistently finds fault-tolerant circuits for all of these tasks, each verified by an exhaustive check over faults.

infographic.key_insight: An LLM guided by a circuit verifier evolves programs that generate fault-tolerant Clifford circuits for multiple encoded quantum-computing tasks.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could reduce manual circuit-design effort for logical state preparation, logical gates, code-switching, and code growth.
method: Frame circuit design as agentic evolutionary program synthesis.
Use an LLM’s pretrained knowledge and tool-use capabilities to evolve circuit-generating programs.
Guide the search with a circuit verifier and exhaustively check faults.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports fault-tolerant circuits for all curated tasks considered, each verified by exhaustive fault checking, but gives no quantitative benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: Scalability of exhaustive fault verification to larger codes and circuits remains unclear from the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Agentic AI for Discovering Fault-Tolerant Quantum Circuits

title: SCOPE: A Physical Execution Latency-Guided Quantum Circuit Compilation Framework
authors: Bolin Zhang, Zhiyuan Zhang, Yongguang Lv, Ruiqing He, Hengliang Guo, Jiandong Shang
abstract: Quantum computing requires compilers to translate algorithms represented in the quantum circuit model into unitary operations supported by physical devices. Limited coherence time makes physical execution latency an important compilation objective. Gate fusion can shorten pulses, but gate count and depth do not capture fused targets' control demands. Evaluating every candidate with quantum optimal control (QOC) would embed pulse optimization in structural search. We present Schmidt-guided Compilation for Optimized Pulse Execution (SCOPE), driven by an operator Schmidt time surrogate. The target's angular distance from product operators measures the required nonlocal change; dividing it by a coupling-limited evolution-rate bound gives a lower bound on exact implementation time. Trace-angle and waveform constraints complete block scores for critical-path evaluation during genetic search. Local QOC determines final pulse durations. Under a numerical nearest-neighbor control model, all 104 results across 13 instances from four application families have shorter QOC critical-path durations than an adapted efficient pulse generation framework with advanced synthesis for quantum circuits (EPOC). Using eight-run instance means, the equally weighted reduction is 42.50\%, with a geometric mean speedup of 2.00. In a shared six-qubit quantum Fourier transform (QFT) ablation, time-surrogate guidance reduces mean QOC duration by 22.21\% relative to gate-count guidance and 21.01\% relative to depth guidance, validating the surrogate's joint use in fitness evaluation and mutation-region selection.

infographic.key_insight: SCOPE guides quantum circuit compilation with a physics-based execution-time surrogate rather than gate count or depth alone.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Optimizing pulse execution latency can help fit quantum computations within limited coherence times.
method: Estimate nonlocal implementation time using operator Schmidt angular distance and a coupling-limited evolution-rate bound.
Combine trace-angle and waveform constraints with critical-path scoring to guide genetic search and mutation-region selection.
Use local quantum optimal control (QOC) to determine final pulse durations.
infographic.evidence_signal: Under a numerical nearest-neighbor control model, all 104 results across 13 instances beat adapted EPOC on QOC critical-path duration, with a 42.50% equally weighted reduction across eight-run instance means and a 2.00× geometric mean speedup.
infographic.watch_item: Results are numerical and control-model-specific; hardware performance and the computational cost of final QOC optimization require validation.
infographic.paper_title: SCOPE: A Physical Execution Latency-Guided Quantum Circuit Compilation Framework

title: Benchmarking memory and nonlinear processing capacity of quantum recurrent neural networks for time series prediction
authors: José Daniel Viqueira, Andrés Gómez, David Mera
abstract: Quantum machine learning has emerged as a promising approach to time series prediction. While quantum reservoir computing has been widely explored for this setting, variational quantum models tailored to sequential data remain comparatively understudied, largely because they are difficult to train. In this work, we present a rigorous benchmark of variational quantum recurrent neural networks (QRNNs) on time series prediction tasks, focusing on two key capabilities: memory and nonlinear processing. We introduce a task-driven methodology that quantifies model capacity, enabling an intuitive and fair comparison across architectures, including classical recurrent baselines. We evaluate the proposed framework on two generic benchmark tasks and on a synthetic dataset describing a chaotic system. Overall, the quantum models achieve performance comparable to their classical counterparts, but classical models scale better with the memory size within the range studied. Notably, one QRNN variant shows higher average capacity on the task designed to jointly probe memory and nonlinear capacity. Moreover, our results show that quantum models offer better capacity when we are able to find a good parameter initialization. However, the increasing sensitivity to initialization leads to a lower probability of finding good solutions as the model size increases. These results provide a principled starting point for designing richer quantum recurrent architectures and for assessing where they may offer practical benefits.

infographic.key_insight: Variational quantum recurrent neural networks match classical performance overall, with one variant showing higher average capacity on a joint memory–nonlinearity task.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Task-driven capacity benchmarks help engineers compare quantum and classical recurrent architectures before selecting models for time series prediction.
method: Benchmark memory and nonlinear processing capacity using a task-driven framework.
Compare variational quantum recurrent architectures with classical recurrent baselines.
Assess how model size and parameter initialization affect performance.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation uses two generic benchmark tasks and a synthetic chaotic-system dataset; classical models scale better with memory size over the studied range.
infographic.watch_item: Quantum model performance is increasingly sensitive to initialization as model size grows, reducing the likelihood of finding good solutions.
infographic.paper_title: Benchmarking memory and nonlinear processing capacity of quantum recurrent neural networks for time series prediction

title: Quantum sine imaginary-time evolution: sequential and QSVT implementations of a probabilistic ground-state filter
authors: Victor A. Penas, Tamara Bottazzi, Marcelo Losada, Diego Tielas, Federico Holik
abstract: We propose quantum sine imaginary-time evolution (QSITE), a quantum algorithm for preparing ground states of a Hamiltonian. QSITE approximates imaginary-time evolution through an exact sine filter. We give two circuit implementations of this operator: a sequential one that applies it as a concatenation of linear combinations of unitaries (LCU), reusing two ancilla qubits across steps via mid-circuit measurement, and a coherent one based on the quantum singular value transformation (QSVT). A telescoping identity shows the two prepare the same state and succeed with identical probability, differing only in how that probability can be boosted. QSITE belongs to the family of ancilla-based probabilistic imaginary-time filters and we state rigorous convergence guarantees: we prove that the QSITE operator converges uniformly to the exact ITE operator, that the prepared state converges to the ideal ITE state, and that the filter probability increases monotonically with each concatenation step. Although the construction applies to an arbitrary Hamiltonian, we specialize it to optimization Hamiltonians, and this specialization is what exposes its structure more easily. Since MaxCut eigenvalues are integers, the probability of failure is periodic in the evolution time, yielding safe zones, the first located analytically and the second numerically. For MaxCut we further show that, when the tolerated energy error is a fixed fraction of the ground-state energy, the probability of failure can be bounded below 1/2 with concatenation steps growing linearly with the number of qubits in the first safe zone. We present numerical results for random Erdös-Rényi instances with up to 24 qubits and benchmark QSITE against QAOA.

infographic.key_insight: QSITE uses an exact sine filter to approximate imaginary-time evolution, with sequential and coherent implementations that prepare the same state with identical success probability.
infographic.engineering_relevance: QSITE offers two ground-state preparation designs with different resource and probability-boosting requirements: ancilla-reusing sequential LCU circuits and coherent QSVT circuits.
method: Concatenate linear combinations of unitaries, reusing two ancillas through mid-circuit measurement.
Implement the equivalent filter coherently using quantum singular value transformation.
Prove convergence to ideal imaginary-time evolution and identify favorable evolution-time zones for MaxCut.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports simulations of random Erdős–Rényi MaxCut instances up to 24 qubits, benchmarking against QAOA, and a bound keeping failure probability below 1/2 under specified error and timing conditions.
infographic.watch_item: The MaxCut failure bound is conditional, and the abstract does not establish hardware performance or an advantage over QAOA.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum sine imaginary-time evolution: sequential and QSVT implementations of a probabilistic ground-state filter

title: Resolving and Suppressing Temporally Correlated Noise in Quantum Error Correction
authors: Alec Eickbusch, Nick Noll, Michael Newman, Matt McEwen, Leigh S. Martin, Alexis Morvan
abstract: Scaling fault-tolerant quantum error correction (QEC) requires suppressing errors in both space and time, yet standard logical memory experiments primarily probe spatial faults. Here, we use a 105-qubit Willow superconducting quantum processor to realize and scale the surface code stability experiment, which is alternatively sensitive to temporal error chains. Scaling from patch sizes of $3 \times 3$ to $7 \times 7$, we realize a timelike block suppression factor of $μ_T = 1.47 \pm 0.25$, demonstrating the ability to maintain temporal error suppression as the number of qubits increases. By extending the stability experiment for many cycles, we uncover a sum-of-exponentials behavior in error suppression caused by a temporally correlated error: data-qubit heating to the third excited state $|3\rangle$. We fully capture this effect with a parameter-free, device-level leakage model incorporating higher-state transport during syndrome extraction cycles. To suppress this error, we develop and realize a walking stability circuit, reaching a logical error probability floor of $\le 3.20\times 10^{-8}$ at 60 cycles---two orders of magnitude below the standard construction---and limited by ionizing radiation error bursts. Finally, by adaptively terminating syndrome extraction based on decoder confidence in an offline analysis, we reduce spacetime logical error by 38% and time overhead by 34% compared to the optimal fixed-cycle strategy.

infographic.key_insight: A walking surface-code stability circuit suppresses temporally correlated leakage errors, reaching a logical error probability floor of ≤3.20×10⁻⁸ at 60 cycles.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Controlling higher-state leakage and adapting syndrome-extraction duration could reduce logical errors and time overhead in fault-tolerant quantum processors.
method: Scale stability experiments from 3×3 to 7×7 patches on a 105-qubit Willow processor.
Model data-qubit heating into |3⟩ and higher-state transport with a parameter-free device-level leakage model.
Implement walking stability circuits and evaluate decoder-confidence-based stopping offline.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments achieved timelike suppression μ_T=1.47±0.25 and a walking-circuit error floor two orders of magnitude below the standard circuit; offline adaptive stopping reduced spacetime logical error by 38% and time overhead by 34%.
infographic.watch_item: Ionizing-radiation error bursts limited the walking circuit, and adaptive stopping was evaluated offline rather than demonstrated in real-time control.
infographic.paper_title: Resolving and Suppressing Temporally Correlated Noise in Quantum Error Correction

title: Specifying & Verifying Quantum Error-Correcting Codes
authors: Stavan Jain, Nithin Raveendran, Aws Albarghouthi
abstract: Building quantum computers is challenging due to the noise that affects qubits. Quantum error correction tackles noise by encoding information in quantum error-correcting (QEC) codes. These codes are often complex, increasingly found by computational search, presented in diverse formalisms with informal arguments, and hard to reason about algorithmically. Given that the rest of the quantum computing stack relies on a QEC code's properties for correct computation, we propose a formally verified foundation for QEC codes. We present QECLean, a Lean-based framework for formally specifying and verifying QEC codes. QECLean backs every claimed QEC-code property with a machine-checked proof, unifies the diverse presentations of codes in the literature through common abstractions, and makes new codes easy to specify. We present a new compositional technique, code combinators, for proving code distance analytically. Code combinators allow us to prove the distance of large codes that are out of reach for algorithmic techniques; for example, we show that IBM's $[[360, 12, \leq 24]]$ code has distance 24, which was previously only known as an upper bound. Furthermore, we show how our approach allows us to formalize and prove entire code families, such as the surface code. Our work lays the foundation required for reasoning about circuit-level implementations of codes on given architectures and for building end-to-end verified compilers for quantum computers. QECLean is available at https://github.com/Stavan-Jain/QECLean

infographic.key_insight: QECLean uses machine-checked proofs to verify quantum error-correcting code properties, including an exact distance of 24 for IBM’s [[360, 12]] code.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Verified code specifications provide a foundation for reasoning about circuit implementations and building end-to-end verified quantum compilers.
method: Specify and verify QEC codes in Lean using common abstractions.
Compose analytical distance proofs with code combinators.
Formalize entire code families, including surface codes.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports proving IBM’s [[360, 12]] code has distance 24, previously known only as an upper bound, and formalizing and proving properties of code families such as the surface code.
infographic.watch_item: Code-level proofs alone do not establish correctness of hardware-specific circuits or an end-to-end quantum compiler.
infographic.paper_title: Specifying & Verifying Quantum Error-Correcting Codes

title: Advancing Quantum Reinforcement Learning with Differentiable Quantum Architecture Search and Adaptive Non-local Observables
authors: Junghoon Justin Park, Kyumin Lee, Anna Jung, Samuel Yen-Chi Chen, Huan-Hsin Tseng, Shinjae Yoo
abstract: Quantum Reinforcement Learning (QRL) using variational quantum circuits (VQCs) is constrained by fixed measurement protocols and hand-designed circuit ansätze. Adaptive Non-local Observables (ANO) and Differentiable Quantum Architecture Search (DiffQAS) address these issues independently, but to our knowledge have not been combined or compared in a single QRL framework. We present an ablation of ANO and DiffQAS within the Quantum Time-series Transformer (QTSTransformer), evaluated on a 2 x 2 factorial design across six environments--two classic-control tasks and four Atari 2600 games. Three findings emerge. First, the quantum agent outperforms a matched classical transformer baseline on five of six environments, with absolute scores ranging from 360.0 vs 304.0 (MarioBros) to 17.2 vs 2.5 (Breakout), while using approximately 12.5x fewer transformer parameters on the four Atari environments (more modestly so on the two classic-control tasks). Second, ANO and DiffQAS provide complementary benefits: ANO yields the largest gain on continuous-state CartPole (347.7 vs 223.2), while DiffQAS yields the largest absolute Atari gains (Breakout 17.2 vs 3.0; DonkeyKong 70.0 vs 37.0). Third, combining both innovations exhibits an asymmetric interaction: ANO-dominant tasks tolerate DiffQAS, whereas DiffQAS-dominant tasks degrade when ANO is added. These results provide design guidance for QRL agents: select between ANO and DiffQAS according to whether the bottleneck is the measurement basis or the gate topology, rather than applying both indiscriminately.

infographic.key_insight: Adaptive measurements and differentiable circuit search offer complementary QRL gains, but combining them can hurt tasks that benefit most from circuit search.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Choose ANO or DiffQAS according to whether measurement basis or gate topology limits performance, rather than enabling both by default.
method: Integrate Adaptive Non-local Observables (ANO) and Differentiable Quantum Architecture Search (DiffQAS) into QTSTransformer.
Use a 2 × 2 factorial ablation to test each innovation alone and together.
Evaluate on two classic-control tasks and four Atari 2600 games against a matched classical transformer.
infographic.evidence_signal: The quantum agent outperformed the classical baseline on five of six environments, including Breakout (17.2 vs 2.5), while using approximately 12.5× fewer transformer parameters on Atari.
infographic.watch_item: Lower transformer parameter counts do not establish runtime or hardware quantum advantage; the abstract does not report execution costs or noise robustness.
infographic.paper_title: Advancing Quantum Reinforcement Learning with Differentiable Quantum Architecture Search and Adaptive Non-local Observables

title: Closing the loop on memory: accurate, shallow and transferable decoding of quantum LDPC codes
authors: Zhou You, Ying Li, Xiao Yuan, Yuan Yao
abstract: Quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes have attracted interest for fault-tolerant quantum computing because their high-rate constructions offer a route to reduced qubit overhead. Realizing this potential requires reliable decoding. Belief propagation (BP) forms the basis of many qLDPC decoders, but can fail to converge under circuit-level noise. Memory-based variants can improve convergence, yet selecting memory strengths that work reliably across different syndromes remains challenging. Here we introduce TEMPO-BP, which adapts each variable's memory strength to the evolving decoding state through local feedback. On the gross code at a physical error rate of 0.4%, single-run TEMPO-BP achieves a per-shot logical failure rate of 0.73%, compared with 2.51% for BP+OSD+CS-10. Ensembles of 10-15 concurrent instances match or lower failure counts relative to Relay-BP-5 at all ten tested operating points, with per-instance iteration caps at least tenfold lower than its serial limit. Without retuning, the gross-code parameters yield fewer observed failures than Relay-BP-5 in its published gross-code configuration across four additional code families. Ablations support state-dependent memory control, while a loop-gain analysis characterizes specific amplification modes in the decoding dynamics.

infographic.key_insight: TEMPO-BP improves quantum LDPC decoding by adapting each variable’s memory strength through local feedback from the evolving decoding state.
infographic.engineering_relevance: More reliable decoding with shallow concurrent runs could help realize qLDPC codes’ potential to reduce fault-tolerant quantum computing overhead.
method: Use state-dependent local feedback to control memory strength in belief propagation.
Run ensembles of 10–15 concurrent decoder instances with reduced per-instance iteration caps.
Assess memory control through ablations and characterize amplification modes with loop-gain analysis.
infographic.evidence_signal: On the gross code at 0.4% physical error, single-run TEMPO-BP achieved 0.73% per-shot logical failure versus 2.51% for BP+OSD+CS-10; ensembles matched or lowered Relay-BP-5 failure counts at all ten tested operating points with at least tenfold lower per-instance iteration caps.
infographic.watch_item: Lower iteration caps do not alone establish lower hardware latency or total resource cost, particularly when running concurrent ensembles.
infographic.paper_title: Closing the loop on memory: accurate, shallow and transferable decoding of quantum LDPC codes

title: Quantum adiabatic and diabatic optimization: A Hilbert space engineering strategy with Rydberg arrays
authors: Rui Lin
abstract: Neutral-atom arrays provide a versatile platform for encoding combinatorial optimization problems with arbitrary graph connectivity [Nguyen et al., PRX Quantum 4, 010316 (2023)]. Although the dynamics of individual encoding gadgets has been studied [Bombieri et al., PRX Quantum 6, 020306 (2025)], understanding annealing bottlenecks in larger networks remains challenging. We investigate how engineering the Hilbert-space geometry controls quantum annealing in a family of blockaded-chain models motivated by these encodings. While boundary terms encode the target maximum independent set problem, the bulk geometry induces an auxiliary optimization problem associated with independent sets of cliques. Spectrally, the energetics of the quantum system can be approximated by physically derived clique weights. When the target problem and the auxiliary problems are consistent, the low-energy modes lie predominantly within the target subspace. This spectral structure motivates a diabatic annealing strategy that exploits target-compatible excited states, as tested on the diamond-chain graph family. These results provide a framework for predicting annealing bottlenecks, and demonstrate Hilbert-space engineering as a strategy for improving neutral-atom quantum optimization protocols.

infographic.key_insight: Engineering Hilbert-space geometry can align low-energy states with target optimization solutions and enable diabatic annealing through target-compatible excited states.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This framework could guide neutral-atom Rydberg-array designs and annealing protocols by identifying geometry-induced optimization bottlenecks.
method: Study blockaded-chain models whose boundary terms encode a target maximum independent set problem.
Model bulk-induced auxiliary problems using independent sets of cliques and physically derived clique weights.
Test a diabatic strategy that exploits target-compatible excited states on diamond-chain graphs.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports approximate spectral modeling and tests on diamond-chain graphs, but provides no numerical performance gains or hardware benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: Benefits depend on consistency between target and auxiliary problems; applicability beyond the studied graph family remains uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum adiabatic and diabatic optimization: A Hilbert space engineering strategy with Rydberg arrays

title: Pulse-timing errors in exchange-only spin qubits: how one control imperfection propagates to VQE, QAOA and fault-tolerance primitives
authors: Yuichiro Minato
abstract: In an exchange-only (EO) spin qubit every gate is a sequence of Heisenberg exchange pulses whose only continuous parameter is the pulse area. We ask how an error in that area propagates to an algorithm's result. On up to six encoded qubits we compile VQE for H$_2$ and LiH, QAOA MaxCut, Grover search, phase estimation and a distance-3 repetition code into exchange pulses and perturb every pulse with a systematic fractional error $\varepsilon$, an offset or per-pulse jitter. For circuits whose first-order response is negligible at the threshold, the useful regime ends at $\varepsilon$ of a few $10^{-3}$: chemical accuracy is lost at $\approx6\times10^{-3}$ for both molecules and 5% of success probability between 3 and $9\times10^{-3}$ for 498-1216 pulses. A systematic error accumulates as the square of the depth and biases the answer; jitter accumulates linearly and, within statistics, does not bias phase estimation. Leakage from inter-block pulses is a third of the CNOT error, survives variational re-optimisation and a leakage-controlled entangler, and makes a leakage-blind repetition-code round worse than its uncorrected data by a factor 38-93 at $\varepsilon=10^{-2}$ in three of four compilations; in the fourth the uncorrected data already fail. The compilation moves the thresholds by a factor of two to eight. Measured over-rotation and exchange noise put devices at the edge of this regime, and with the measured 3.5 $μ$s $T_2^*$ a quasi-static magnetic gradient limits thousand-pulse circuits unless $J/h$ reaches several hundred MHz with continuous areas, because a duration grid of 2-5% of the SWAP time starts to cost chemical accuracy. As a bit budget, a common-mode area error needs 8-10 significant bits and a 6-bit significand for the durations suffices in the tested circuits; half-precision words and picosecond timers exceed this; older devices had 6-8 bits of analog stability.

infographic.key_insight: Small exchange-pulse area errors can undermine encoded quantum algorithms, with systematic errors accumulating quadratically in circuit depth and jitter accumulating linearly.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Exchange-only spin-qubit control needs roughly 8–10 significant bits for common-mode pulse-area accuracy, alongside leakage mitigation and sufficient exchange speed to limit magnetic-gradient effects.
method: Compiled VQE, QAOA, Grover search, phase estimation and a distance-3 repetition code into exchange pulses on up to six encoded qubits.
Perturbed pulse areas using systematic fractional errors, offsets and per-pulse jitter.
Evaluated algorithm accuracy, leakage, compilation sensitivity and control-resolution requirements.
infographic.evidence_signal: In the tested circuits, chemical accuracy failed near a systematic fractional error of 0.006 for H₂ and LiH, while 498–1,216-pulse circuits lost 5% of success probability at errors of 0.003–0.009.
infographic.watch_item: Thresholds varied by factors of 2–8 across compilations, and leakage-blind error correction could worsen performance; these small-circuit results are not universal fault-tolerance thresholds.
infographic.paper_title: Pulse-timing errors in exchange-only spin qubits: how one control imperfection propagates to VQE, QAOA and fault-tolerance primitives

title: Quantum Loading of Charge and Spin-Adapted MPS
authors: Matthew R. Hennefarth, Lesley Gover, Carys Harvey, Zheting Jin, Ryan Levy, Sukin Sim
abstract: Matrix product states (MPS) are powerful classical representations of correlated quantum states, but loading a large bond dimension MPS can substantially increase the cost in fault-tolerant quantum algorithms. We develop a circuit for preparing a U(1)~$\times$~SU(2)-symmetric MPS directly from spin-adapted reduced tensors. Using Householder--LKS synthesis, the circuit prepares each symmetry-allowed reduced block and applies Clebsch--Gordan coefficients to recover the magnetic degrees of freedom, avoiding explicit loading of the corresponding unfolded dense tensors. The reduced-tensor data loading is dominant in cost. We benchmark $4 \times 4$ and $4 \times 6$ Fermi--Hubbard states and active-space models of \ce{[Fe2S2]^2-}, \ce{[Fe4S4]^2-}, and low- and high-spin cytochrome P450. At 15-bit rotation precision, the molecular benchmarks show $\sim 14\times$ to $54\times$ Toffoli reductions, $\sim 20\times$ to $87\times$ active volume reduction, and $\sim 33\times$ to $140\times$ volume (Toffoli $\times$ qubits) reduction at the QROM-optimal point, relative to dense MPS loading. Fermi--Hubbard speedups increase with bond dimension and track the inverse tensor density, with modest qubit overhead. However, while we discuss generalization of our algorithm to reduce cost given further symmetry or using more performant unitary synthesis methods, extrapolation to larger lattices suggests that DMRG-state loading may exceed downstream phase-estimation costs, motivating co-design of state fidelity, compression, and the initial-state ansatz.

infographic.key_insight: Preparing charge- and spin-adapted matrix product states directly from reduced tensors avoids dense tensor loading and substantially lowers quantum state-preparation costs.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Symmetry-aware loading can reduce fault-tolerant quantum resource requirements for correlated-electron simulations, although state preparation may still dominate downstream computation.
method: Load symmetry-allowed reduced blocks of a U(1) × SU(2)-symmetric MPS using Householder–LKS synthesis.
Apply Clebsch–Gordan coefficients to reconstruct magnetic degrees of freedom.
Avoid explicitly loading unfolded dense tensors.
infographic.evidence_signal: Benchmarks cover 4 × 4 and 4 × 6 Fermi–Hubbard states and molecular active spaces; at 15-bit rotation precision and the QROM-optimal point, molecular cases show approximately 14–54× fewer Toffolis, 20–87× lower active volume, and 33–140× lower Toffoli × qubit volume than dense MPS loading.
infographic.watch_item: Larger-lattice extrapolations suggest DMRG-state loading may exceed phase-estimation costs, motivating joint optimization of state fidelity, compression, and the initial-state ansatz.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum Loading of Charge and Spin-Adapted MPS

title: Certifying quantum generative models beyond the Fisher trace
authors: Vicente Leyton-Ortega, Kathleen Hamilton
abstract: Whether a trained quantum generative model has learned its target is usually decided by a diagnostic validated on a labeled benchmark, and such a diagnostic can pass that validation by recovering how the benchmark was built. We analyze Fisher-trace and kernel-based certification of the real-amplitude quantum circuit Born machine in noiseless statevector simulation. For real-amplitude circuits built from half-angle rotations, the classical Fisher information equals the quantum Fisher information almost everywhere, so its trace equals the parameter count and carries no information about fit quality. The Fisher eigenvalue rank counts the live nodes of the amplitude tree: it coincides with the label on a sparse benchmark and is uninformative on a full-support one. The pooled Wasserstein and maximum-mean-discrepancy scores move with optimizer convergence and with the scoring convention. For two bitstring defect families on which both metrics have closed forms, we compute the tolerance-mismatch window in which the discrepancy rejects generators that the transport threshold admits; it opens only at certification-grade tolerances and closes as the qubit number grows. On the Hamming cost we prove a sharp tolerance ratio above which the discrepancy vote is redundant, and we obtain the exact worst-parity minimax value over all unit-diagonal positive-semidefinite kernels, which is exponentially small in the qubit number. In a numerical campaign at the tolerances a near-term experiment can resolve, the discrepancy vote changed no verdict at a thousand shots or more. The false-pass guarantee does not extend to device noise.

infographic.key_insight: For the studied real-amplitude quantum generative circuits, the Fisher trace counts parameters rather than measuring fit, while kernel discrepancy adds no certification benefit in the reported shot-resolved tests.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Certification should test distributional accuracy directly and check whether combined metrics provide independent evidence rather than reflect circuit structure or benchmark construction.
method: Analyze Fisher information and amplitude-tree rank in noiseless statevector simulations.
Derive Wasserstein–discrepancy tolerance windows for two bitstring defect families.
Prove Hamming-cost redundancy bounds and an exponentially small worst-parity kernel minimax value.
infographic.evidence_signal: At experimentally resolvable tolerances, the numerical campaign found that the discrepancy vote changed no verdict at 1,000 shots or more.
infographic.watch_item: The false-pass guarantee does not extend to device noise, and pooled scores depend on optimizer convergence and scoring convention.
infographic.paper_title: Certifying quantum generative models beyond the Fisher trace

title: Quantum algorithmic framework for finite element analysis of isotropic linear elastic materials via efficient block-encoding
authors: Yuki Sato, Ruho Kondo
abstract: Quantum computing offers a promising approach to accelerating large-scale numerical analysis, including the finite element method. However, its practical application requires efficient quantum circuit implementations of discretized linear systems. In this study, we develop a quantum algorithmic framework for two-dimensional isotropic linear elastic materials discretized using the finite element method. The key contribution is an explicit construction of a normalized block-encoding of the shifted global stiffness matrix, which is essential for applying a quantum linear system solver based on the quantum singular value transformation with improved dependence on the condition number. By analytically diagonalizing the element stiffness matrix and expressing the global stiffness matrix through a factorized finite element assembly, we construct the required block-encoding using a constant number of ancilla qubits and a gate complexity logarithmic in the number of degrees of freedom. We further analyze the computational complexity of displacement state preparation, strain energy estimation, and low-resolution displacement reconstruction, identifying conditions under which polynomial quantum speedups may be achieved. Numerical experiments on cantilever beam problems verify the accuracy of the proposed quantum circuits and demonstrate agreement with conventional finite element solutions. These results establish an explicit and resource-efficient quantum framework for finite element analysis of isotropic linear elastic materials.

infographic.key_insight: An explicit block-encoding of the shifted finite element stiffness matrix enables a resource-efficient quantum framework for 2D isotropic linear elasticity.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework identifies conditions for polynomial quantum speedups in displacement state preparation, strain energy estimation, and low-resolution displacement reconstruction.
method: Analytically diagonalize element stiffness matrices and factorize global finite element assembly.
Construct normalized block-encoding with constant ancilla count and gate complexity logarithmic in the number of degrees of freedom.
Use quantum singular value transformation for linear-system solving with improved condition-number dependence.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical cantilever beam experiments verify the proposed circuits and show agreement with conventional finite element solutions.
infographic.watch_item: Speedups are conditional; efficient block-encoding alone does not establish end-to-end advantage for loading inputs or reconstructing full displacement fields.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum algorithmic framework for finite element analysis of isotropic linear elastic materials via efficient block-encoding

title: Static Bounds on Thermal Fast Scrambling
authors: Yixuan Ma, Weikang Li, Dong-Ling Deng
abstract: Scrambling, the process by which initially localized quantum information spreads across an interacting many-body system, is a hallmark of quantum chaos and plays a central role in understanding black hole dynamics. In thermal systems, the chaos bound of Maldacena, Shenker and Stanford limits the exponential growth rate of out-of-time-order correlations to $2π/β$, assuming that time-ordered correlation functions factorize after a dissipation time. Establishing the corresponding rigorous logarithmic lower bounds on scrambling times at arbitrary fixed temperature has remained an open problem, most notably in disordered systems, where the Gibbs state depends on the same random couplings that drive the dynamics. Here we prove such bounds at every fixed temperature for the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev (SYK) model and for random $k$-local spin systems, without assuming real-time factorization. Our approach uses the operator-size distribution of the square root of the Gibbs state to quantify how local probes modify its structure. This static information bounds the thermal correlator uniformly in time along the edges of its analytic strip in complex time, and analyticity then limits how rapidly scrambling can develop. For both families of models, we prove that with probability tending to one the scrambling time is at least $(1-ε)[β/(2π)]\log N$ for any $0<ε<1$, with the coefficient $β/(2π)$ suggested by the chaos bound. The bound holds for each fixed pair of distinct Majorana modes in the SYK model and for the target average of any fixed single-site source in the spin model. These results place the thermal fast-scrambling timescale on a rigorous footing and show how static properties of the Gibbs state can constrain real-time information spreading.

infographic.key_insight: Static properties of thermal Gibbs states rigorously limit how quickly quantum information can scramble in SYK and random k-local spin models.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The results provide theoretical timescale benchmarks for thermal information spreading in quantum simulations of these models.
method: Analyze the operator-size distribution of the square root of the Gibbs state.
Use this static structure to bound thermal correlators along complex-time analytic-strip edges.
Apply analyticity to constrain scrambling without assuming real-time factorization.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports proofs that, at every fixed positive temperature and with probability tending to one as N grows, scrambling takes at least (1−ε)[β/(2π)] log N for any 0<ε<1.
infographic.watch_item: These are asymptotic lower bounds for specific random-model observables, not guarantees of achievable scrambling speeds or finite-device performance.
infographic.paper_title: Static Bounds on Thermal Fast Scrambling

title: Reinforcement Learning designs Quantum Repeater Protocols on Networks beyond the Chain Scenario
authors: Andrés Agustí Casado, Álvaro Troyano Olivas, Javier Faba García, Luis M. Robledo, Vicente Martín, Laura Ortiz
abstract: Small-scale quantum repeater protocols have been shown to distribute entanglement over existing telecommunication infrastructure by means of short range quantum communications and long range classical messages. For larger networks, there are a number of theoretical proposals about how to operate the network to achieve a good performance under varying metrics. Moreover, since the dimension of the space of possible protocols grows exponentially with network size, plenty of those proposals are based on heuristics that reduce the search space. One of these is entanglement routing, which simplifies the problem on non-linear networks by allocating a series of disjoint paths and running chain protocols simultaneously on them. However, in this work we claim routing leads to suboptimal protocols. In fact, inspired by works on linear chains, we apply reinforcement learning to non-linear networks and optimize over the larger non-routing protocol space. Then, we find protocols that outperform a routed extension of the swap-ASAP protocol, even in the parameter regimes where the latter is widely recognized as the state of the art. These results indicate that routing must be discarded in favor of non-routing methods, while they pave the way towards the design of a sensible Quantum Internet architecture.

infographic.key_insight: Reinforcement learning discovers quantum repeater protocols on non-linear networks that outperform a routed swap-ASAP baseline by searching beyond disjoint-path routing.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Quantum network control architectures may benefit from supporting non-routing operations rather than restricting entanglement distribution to independent chains.
method: Apply reinforcement learning to protocol design on non-linear quantum repeater networks.
Optimize over a broader protocol space than disjoint-path entanglement routing allows.
Compare learned protocols with a routed extension of swap-ASAP.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports improved performance over routed swap-ASAP even in parameter regimes where that baseline is considered state of the art, but provides no numerical gains or evaluation scale.
infographic.watch_item: Scalability remains a concern because the protocol search space grows exponentially with network size.
infographic.paper_title: Reinforcement Learning designs Quantum Repeater Protocols on Networks beyond the Chain Scenario

title: Quantum-Assisted D-FACTS Scheduling for Moving Target Defense under Switching Limits
authors: Hongyu Wu, Yichen Liu, Bo Liu
abstract: Moving target defense with distributed flexible alternating-current transmission system (D-FACTS) devices re- quires activation decisions as operating points change. Switching limits couple these decisions, but period-by-period rankings can overlook combinations needed to complete low-activation schedules. This paper proposes cross-period candidate sharing and schedule-completion evaluation to allocate limited physical checks in quantum-assisted D-FACTS scheduling. The quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) generates activation candidates, while classical scheduling enforces operating and switching constraints. We also quantify model-based activation requirements and test detection through noisy nonlinear trials. A modified IEEE 118-bus study assesses recovery of reference activation and switching objectives within the evaluated set. Combining candidate sharing and schedule-completion evaluation improves final-budget recovery over period-by-period ranking in the primary operating window for every tested candidate generator. The results show that quantum and classical candidates yield identical recovery curves under combined checking, so the same allocation policy applies to either source.

infographic.key_insight: Sharing activation candidates across periods and evaluating schedule completion improves recovery of low-activation, switching-constrained D-FACTS schedules regardless of candidate source.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach helps allocate limited physical checks when scheduling grid moving target defense under operating and device-switching constraints.
method: Generate activation candidates with QAOA or classical alternatives.
Share candidates across periods and prioritize checks using schedule-completion evaluation.
Use classical scheduling to enforce operating and switching constraints.
infographic.evidence_signal: In a modified IEEE 118-bus study, combined checking improved final-budget reference-objective recovery for every tested generator in the primary operating window, with identical recovery curves for quantum and classical candidates.
infographic.watch_item: Results are limited to the evaluated candidate set and operating windows and do not establish a quantum advantage.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum-Assisted D-FACTS Scheduling for Moving Target Defense under Switching Limits

title: $Q$-Drive: A Hybrid Quantum-Classical Control Framework for Nonlinear Vehicular Dynamics
authors: Muhammad Al-Zafar Khan, Safaa Alqrinawi, Jamal Al-Karaki, Omar Alhussein, Saif Al-Kuwari, Ahmed Farouk
abstract: In this paper, we introduce $Q$-Drive, a hybrid quantum-classical control framework for nonlinear vehicular dynamics that integrates variational quantum circuits (VQCs) with classical optimization, encoding vehicle states into a quantum Hilbert space via angle embedding, applying a trainable quantum ansatz to generate control signals, and refining circuit parameters through gradient descent to minimize tracking error and control effort. The proposed $Q$-Drive is evaluated in two settings: Single-vehicle control of nonlinear bicycle dynamics and a decoupled multi-vehicle swarm scenario with fleet sizes ranging from $N=2$ to $N=50$, demonstrating that the approach achieves exceptionally low control effort, reduced by orders of magnitude compared to classical model predictive control (MPC) and linear-quadratic regulator (LQR) benchmarks in the single-vehicle case, with average per-vehicle control effort decreasing by over 60\% from $N=2$ to $N=50$ in the swarm setting. Beyond empirical evaluation, we establish rigorous stability guarantees by constructing a composite Lyapunov function that jointly captures classical tracking dynamics and quantum-state purity. This analysis proves that the closed-loop system remains ultimately uniformly bounded under arbitrary road conditions, including inclined, rough, and curvilinear surfaces, as well as in the presence of quantum decoherence on the NISQ hardware, with explicit critical thresholds linking decoherence rates to environmental adversity. For the swarm extension, a theoretical bound is derived that shows that the average per-vehicle control effort decreases inversely with fleet size, in agreement with empirical observations. $Q$-Drive offers a promising direction for intelligent transportation systems by enabling robust, energy-efficient, and scalable vehicle control under complex real-world driving conditions.

infographic.key_insight: Q-Drive combines variational quantum circuits with classical optimization to control nonlinear vehicle dynamics while reporting substantially lower control effort than classical baselines.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework targets energy-efficient vehicle and fleet control, with conditional stability guarantees accounting for road disturbances and quantum decoherence.
method: Encode vehicle states into quantum circuits using angle embedding.
Generate control signals with a trainable quantum ansatz optimized by gradient descent.
Analyze stability using a composite Lyapunov function combining tracking dynamics and quantum-state purity.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports orders-of-magnitude lower single-vehicle control effort versus MPC and LQR, and over 60% lower average per-vehicle effort as decoupled fleet size increases from 2 to 50.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish real-hardware performance or matched tracking accuracy across baselines; decoupled fleet results may not extend to interacting traffic.
infographic.paper_title: $Q$-Drive: A Hybrid Quantum-Classical Control Framework for Nonlinear Vehicular Dynamics
